subject: history_social
passage: Students of Roman history have heard that after destroying Carthage in 146 BCE, the Romans sowed its fields with salt so nothing would grow again. The story appeals as a symbol of total conquest. It has one problem: no ancient writer tells it. Ancient accounts of the destruction mention fire, demolition, and a curse on the site, but not salt; the earliest clear statement of the salting seems to be in a reference work of 1930, after which textbooks repeated it. Nor would it have made sense; salt was valuable, and enough of it to poison farmland would have cost a fortune. The salting of Carthage, it appears, is less an ancient fact than a modern one: a detail invented so recently that we can almost watch its birth.
stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It states a widely repeated claim, shows that the ancient sources do not support it, adds a practical objection, and reinterprets the claim as a modern invention.
choices.B: It describes the destruction of Carthage as ancient historians recorded it and then explains why Rome regarded the city as a threat.
choices.C: It states a widely repeated claim, concedes that it cannot be verified, and suggests that it is nonetheless probably true.
choices.D: It explains how a historical detail spread from textbook to textbook and argues that such errors are common.

explanation.why: The text states the familiar story, grants its appeal, and then raises the problem that "no ancient writer tells it," tracing the claim to a 1930 reference work. It adds a practical objection about the cost of salt and concludes that the salting is "a modern" fact, an invention. The structure is claim, source-based challenge, practical objection, reinterpretation.
explanation.A: Correct. Familiar story, missing ancient sources and a 1930 origin, the cost of salt, and the conclusion that the detail is modern.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The ancient accounts are mentioned only to show what they omit, and the text never discusses why Rome saw Carthage as a threat.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text does not call the story probably true; it concludes that the detail was "invented" in modern times.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The spread through textbooks is one step in the argument, and the text makes no general claim that such errors are common.
